Combine record sets into one

Source: R/combine.R
scopus_combine.Rd

Binds several scopus_records objects into a single one, renumbering entry_number across the result and, optionally, dropping duplicates. This is the safe way to merge separate fetches: plain rbind() would leave duplicate entry numbers, and c() would return a list.

Usage

scopus_combine(..., dedupe = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'scopus_records'
c(x, ...)

Arguments

...

Two or more scopus_records objects, or a single list of them.

dedupe

Whether, and by which rule, to keep once the records that are one record. FALSE, the default, keeps every row. TRUE, also spelled "id_or_shared_doi", treats records as one when they share a 'Scopus' identifier, or when they share a DOI and one of them lacks an identifier. "id_or_doi" also merges records with different identifiers that share a DOI, and "id_then_doi" applies the rule of scopusflow 0.4.0 and earlier. See Details.

x

A scopus_records object (for the c() method).

Value

A scopus_records tibble. Per-retrieval attributes such as total_results and plan are not carried over, since they describe a single fetch. The provenance a merge leaves true is kept, as scopus_fetch_plan() keeps it for plan cells. retrieved_at is the earliest of the inputs' times and retrieved_until the latest, so a baseline merged with its update is dated from one to the other. Every contributing scopusflow_version is listed. The merge itself is recorded in the combined attribute, a list of n_in (records supplied), n_out (records kept), n_removed, deduplicated, rule (the rule applied, NA when none was) and doi_conflicts (how many DOIs records with different identifiers share, NA when no rule was applied). It is what lets scopus_search_report() state how many duplicates were removed and how, so the PRISMA-S item is answered.

Details

De-duplication compares DOIs as scopus_extract_dois() does, without resolver prefixes such as https://doi.org/ or doi: and ignoring case. It keeps the first record of each group, in the order the sets were given, and a record with neither an identifier nor a DOI cannot be matched and is kept.

Under the default rule, records with the same 'Scopus' identifier are one record, and a record without an identifier joins the identified record that carries its DOI. Records with different identifiers are never merged, even when they share a DOI. 'Scopus' holds duplicate records of one paper (Valderrama-Zurián et al., 2015), but it also gives one DOI to distinct papers (Franceschini et al., 2015), and a review loses a wrongly removed record for good where a surviving duplicate is caught at screening. Such DOIs are counted in doi_conflicts, which the search record reports, so that they can be checked by hand. A record without an identifier whose DOI two identified records carry is kept once, apart from both. Records without an identifier that share a DOI no identified record carries are one record.

"id_or_doi" merges every record linked to another by a shared identifier or a shared DOI, directly or through a chain of such links. It suits a set whose shared DOIs have been checked and found to be duplicates. "id_then_doi" keys each record on its identifier, failing that on its DOI lower-cased but not otherwise cleaned, and so reproduces a set de-duplicated by scopusflow 0.4.0 or earlier.

References

Franceschini, F., Maisano, D., & Mastrogiacomo, L. (2015). Errors in DOI indexing by bibliometric databases. Scientometrics, 102(3), 2181–2186. doi:10.1007/s11192-014-1503-4

Valderrama-Zurián, J.-C., Aguilar-Moya, R., Melero-Fuentes, D., & Aleixandre-Benavent, R. (2015). A systematic analysis of duplicate records in Scopus. Journal of Informetrics, 9(3), 570–576. doi:10.1016/j.joi.2015.05.002

See also

scopus_fetch_plan(), which combines plan cells the same way.

Examples

# A baseline retrieval and a later one, merged into a cumulative set. The
# bundled corpus of real articles stands in for both, since 'Scopus'
# records may not be redistributed.
baseline <- example_records[example_records$year <= 2023, ]
later <- example_records
combined <- scopus_combine(baseline, later, dedupe = TRUE)
nrow(combined)
#> [1] 149

# Those records carry no 'Scopus' identifier, so de-duplication falls back
# to the DOI. The eleven that arrived without one cannot be matched, and so
# survive in both copies, which is why 138 distinct articles come back as
# 149 rows.
sum(is.na(example_records$doi))
#> [1] 11
